paras: The lynching of Henry Bird took place near Grayson, in Clinton County, Missouri, in late September 1880, when a search party of local men seized Bird, a Black farm laborer accused of raping his employer's wife, and he was hanged from an elm tree. The story ran as a wire item across the country, often misplaced in Kansas and once giving his name as "Henry Boyd", and a neighboring Missouri paper endorsed the killing.

Bird was described as married and as having worked for three years for Benjamin Winn, "a wealthy stock dealer in Clinton county". Grayson was a small town about twenty-nine miles east of Leavenworth, Kansas, and the Winns lived about a mile and a half outside it. The first Leavenworth dispatch recalled that a Black man jailed at nearby Platte City for raping a white woman had recently been taken out and hanged.

According to a Leavenworth dispatch, Mrs. Winn, about 26, was returning on horseback from Grayson on the afternoon of Friday, September 24, when a man stopped her horse at her gate, pulled her from the saddle, tied her riding habit over her head and raped her. She rode back to Grayson to report it, and within half an hour seventy men, or within an hour two hundred, were searching on horseback. The first dispatch said suspicion fell on a stranger who had been loafing around Grayson and predicted that "the most trivial circumstances" would get him lynched if caught.

The Sept. 27 Leavenworth account said Bird had changed clothes and joined the search, and that near Edgerton Junction a searcher noticed mud on the back of his neck while another brought a man's sock from the scene. The searchers took Bird into custody and made him strip, reporting mud on his back and a sock matching the one found. Passers-by found his body at noon on Sunday, September 26, hanging to a small elm tree near Grayson.
Shorter paragraphs reprinted in October said instead that "a scratch on his neck drew attention" and that his companions "hanged him promptly".
No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution of anyone in the search party appears in the coverage.

Two wire lines carried the story: a Leavenworth correspondent's dispatches and a Plattsburg special to the St. Louis Missouri Republican, which ran in papers from Memphis and Wheeling to St. Paul, Cheyenne and Helena between September 27 and 30. Headline writers cast Bird as a "Negro Ravisher", "A Black Mons'er" and a "Mulatto Miscreant", and the Omaha Bee headlined "A Foul Bird, Whose Carcass Picturesquely Ornaments an Elm Tree". Others framed the killing as "Speedy Justice", "A Condign Punishment" or "Summary Lynching".

Closer to home, the Richmond Democrat of Ray County called the hanging "short work" and argued that swift punishment by a mob was "the only way to stop it". The Chillicothe Crisis reported it in one line among Missouri news. A short paragraph placing the crime in "Clinton county, Kansas" circulated into October in Pennsylvania, Nevada and Georgia weeklies, and by the time it reached the Fayetteville Observer in Tennessee on November 4 the victim had become "Henry Boyd".

The Plattsburg special said Mrs. Winn was dragged into a ravine on her way home from visiting friends and that neighbors overtook the assailant and "hung him on the spot", without mentioning his joining the search. Dates also differ: the Leavenworth reports put the assault on Friday, September 24, while the Richmond Democrat put it on Saturday and the hanging that night; the Leavenworth date is supported by a dispatch of September 25 that already reported the assault.

accounts.label: Leavenworth dispatch (Sept. 25-27)
accounts.gist: A mud-daubed man assaulted Mrs. Winn at her gate; Bird joined the 200-man search, was suspected over mud on his neck and a matching sock, was taken and stripped, and was found hanging to an elm near Grayson at noon Sept. 26.

accounts.label: Missouri Republican's Plattsburg special
accounts.gist: A man dragged Mrs. Winn into a ravine and raped her; 'a party of neighbors' pursued, overtook and hanged him on the spot; he was a married mulatto laborer on Winn's farm.

accounts.label: Richmond Democrat (Ray County, Mo.)
accounts.gist: A Black man raped Mrs. Winn in Clinton county on Saturday and was hanged by a mob that night.

accounts.label: Short wire paragraph
accounts.gist: Bird joined the lynching party, a scratch on his neck drew attention, other evidence convinced his companions, and they hanged him promptly.

framing.detail: The Richmond Democrat called it 'short work' and said 'lustful brutes' must learn that punishment will be 'short and swift ... the only way to stop it'.
The Omaha Bee headlined 'A Foul Bird, Whose Carcass Picturesquely Ornaments an Elm Tree' and 'A Daring Dark Devil'; the Wilmington Gazette 'A Black Mons'er Lynched'.
The Plattsburg special ran under headlines such as 'Speedy Justice by an Infuriated Crowd', 'A Condign Punishment' and 'Summary Lynching of a Missouri Ravisher'.
The Sacramento Record-Union's brief was headed plainly 'Negro Lynched in Missouri'.

conflicts.note: Missouri papers and the Plattsburg dispatch put Grayson and Clinton County in Missouri; the Kansas placement appears in reprints of the Leavenworth-datelined story and is likely a desk error.
'Boyd' appears only in a Nov. 4 Tennessee reprint of a paragraph that earlier printings give as 'Bird'.
